questions.question: can I get a fee waiver for naturalization?
questions.answer:
You may be able to request a fee waiver for the Application for Naturalization (Form N-400) if you can demonstrate an inability to pay [S3]. USCIS evaluates this inability to pay based on whether you or a qualifying household member receive a means-tested benefit, if your household income is at or below 150 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG), or if you are experiencing extreme financial hardship [S6]. Additionally, there are no fees for filing an Application for Naturalization for certain military service members [S7].

The provided sources contain conflicting information regarding the income threshold for fee waivers, reflecting different policy periods. While one source indicates that a rule permitted fee waivers only if household income was at or below 125% of the FPG [S2], another source lists the threshold as 150% of the FPG [S6].

questions.question: I have a disability and cannot learn English. Is there an exception to the English test?
questions.answer: An exception to the English and civics requirements exists for individuals with a physical or developmental disability or mental impairment that has lasted, or is expected to last, at least 12 months [S1]. To qualify, an individual must demonstrate that the disability or impairment affects their functioning such that they are unable to meet the English and civics requirements, even with reasonable accommodations [S1]. This exception requires a licensed medical professional—specifically a medical doctor, doctor of osteopathy, or clinical psychologist—to complete Form N-648, certifying that the disability prevents the individual from meeting the requirements [S1][S7]. This process is distinct from requesting a reasonable accommodation, which modifies the manner in which an applicant meets the educational requirements but does not exempt them from the requirements themselves [S3][S4].

questions.question: I am 68 and have had a green card for 22 years. Do I still have to take the English test?
questions.answer: If you are 65 years of age or older and have resided in the United States as a lawful permanent resident (LPR) for at least 20 years at the time of filing, you are exempt from the English language requirement [S3]. Although you are exempt from the English test, you are still required to meet the civics requirement, for which you may receive special consideration and be administered specially designated test forms [S3][S7].

questions.question: I was outside the United States for eight months. Does that break my continuous residence?
questions.answer: An absence of eight months is considered an absence of more than 6 months but less than 1 year, which creates a presumption that the continuity of residence has been broken [S2][S4]. This is a rebuttable presumption, meaning an applicant may provide evidence to establish that the continuity of residence was not disrupted [S2]. Such evidence may include documentation that the applicant did not terminate U.S. employment, that immediate family members remained in the United States, or that the applicant retained access to or continued to own or lease a home in the United States [S2].

questions.question: USCIS interviewed me over a year ago and still has not decided my case. What can I do?
questions.answer: If USCIS fails to make a decision on a naturalization application within 120 days after the date of the initial examination, an applicant may apply to the United States district court for the district in which they reside for a hearing on the matter [S1][S2][S4][S6]. The district court has jurisdiction to either determine the matter itself or remand the case to USCIS with instructions to make a determination [S2][S4].

questions.question: My naturalization application was denied. Can I appeal it?
questions.answer: If your naturalization application is denied, you may request a hearing before an immigration officer, which serves as an administrative appeal [S4][S7][S8]. If that immigration officer affirms the denial, you may then seek review of the decision in the United States district court for the district in which you reside [S2][S7][S8]. You must exhaust these administrative remedies before you are eligible to seek judicial review in a district court [S2][S3][S6].

questions.question: How long do I have to be married to a U.S. citizen before I can apply for citizenship?
questions.answer:
To be eligible for naturalization as the spouse of a U.S. citizen residing in the United States, you must have been living in marital union with your citizen spouse for at least 3 years immediately preceding the date you file your application [S1][S2][S4]. During this 3-year period, your spouse must have been a U.S. citizen [S2].

If you are applying as the spouse of a U.S. citizen who is regularly stationed abroad in qualifying employment, there is no specified duration of marriage required prior to filing, though you must be married to the citizen spouse at the time of filing [S7][S8].

questions.question: I gave a wrong answer at my interview. Can that count against my good moral character?
questions.answer: Giving a wrong answer during a naturalization interview can negatively impact a finding of good moral character if it qualifies as "false testimony" [S4][S5]. To be considered false testimony that precludes a finding of good moral character, the statement must be an oral statement made under oath with the subjective intent of obtaining immigration or naturalization benefits [S4][S7]. The lie does not need to be material; even an immaterial lie can prevent a finding of good moral character if it was told with the intent to obtain such benefits [S4].

questions.question: Can I still naturalize if I am in removal proceedings?
questions.answer:
USCIS generally lacks the authority to grant naturalization to an applicant against whom a removal proceeding is pending [S1][S7]. If a Notice to Appear (NTA) is issued and a removal proceeding is pending on or before the date of the decision on a naturalization application, USCIS officers are instructed to deny the application [S1]. This applies even if the removal proceeding has been administratively closed, as administrative closure is considered a temporary pause rather than a termination of proceedings [S1].

However, there is disagreement regarding the authority of federal courts to naturalize an applicant while removal proceedings are pending:

*   **Majority View:** Many circuits have held that the statutory language of INA 318 (8 U.S.C. § 1429) precludes district courts from granting naturalization while removal proceedings are pending [S2][S3].
*   **Alternative View:** Some courts have held that while the statute prohibits the Attorney General from considering a naturalization application during pending removal proceedings, it does not impose the same limitation on the courts [S6][S8]. Under this view, courts may have the authority to naturalize an applicant while removal proceedings are pending, though they cannot do so once there is an outstanding final finding of deportability [S6][S8].

Additionally, there is an exception for certain applications for naturalization based on military service [S1][S7].

questions.question: Will two DUI convictions stop me from becoming a citizen?
questions.answer: Two or more convictions for driving under the influence (DUI) during the statutory period establish a rebuttable presumption that an applicant lacks good moral character (GMC) [S1][S6]. This presumption may be overcome if the applicant provides "substantial relevant and credible contrary evidence" that they possessed good moral character during the period in which the DUI offenses were committed and that the convictions were an aberration [S1]. Efforts to reform or rehabilitate after multiple DUI convictions do not, by themselves, demonstrate good moral character during the period that includes the convictions [S1].

questions.question: If I sue because USCIS never decided, can the judge grant my citizenship, or does it go back to USCIS?
questions.answer: Under 8 U.S.C. § 1447(b), if a district court intervenes because USCIS failed to make a determination within 120 days of an examination, the court has the authority to either determine the matter itself or remand it to USCIS with instructions to determine the matter [S2][S5][S7]. However, even if a district court grants a naturalization application, the process is not complete because USCIS retains the "sole authority" to perform the final steps of naturalization, which include administering the oath of allegiance and issuing the certificate of naturalization [S5].

questions.question: Is a notice to appear the same thing as a warrant of arrest for naturalization purposes?
questions.answer:
Whether a "notice to appear" (NTA) is considered the same as a "warrant of arrest" for naturalization purposes is a subject of disagreement among courts and authorities [S7].

*   **The Ninth Circuit's View:** The Ninth Circuit has held that a "warrant of arrest" and a "notice to appear" are distinct documents [S1][S6]. It concluded that a "warrant of arrest" is a writ issued to arrest and detain an alien, whereas a "notice to appear" is akin to a summons that provides information about removal proceedings but does not direct law enforcement to arrest or detain the individual [S1][S2]. Consequently, the Ninth Circuit rejects the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) regulatory interpretation in 8 C.F.R. § 318.1, which treats an NTA as a "warrant of arrest" for the purposes of 8 U.S.C. § 1429 [S6][S8].
*   **The Seventh Circuit's View:** The Seventh Circuit has upheld the DHS regulation, reasoning that an agency may define its own vocabulary and that there is no logical problem with an agency treating a "notice to appear" as a "warrant of arrest" without issuing two separate documents [S5][S7].
*   **DHS Policy:** DHS regulations state that for the purposes of 8 U.S.C. § 1429, a notice to appear issued under 8 C.F.R. part 239 shall be regarded as a warrant of arrest [S3][S7].

questions.question: Can I sue under the Administrative Procedure Act instead of the naturalization review statute?
questions.answer: The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) provides an "elaborate" and "exhaustively detail[ed]" review process for naturalization applications, which Congress intended to collectively and exclusively direct the review of application denials [S7]. APA claims are not exempt from the INA's exhaustion requirements [S1]. Furthermore, the APA is not a jurisdiction-conferring statute [S5]. However, Section 1421(c) specifies that judicial review of a naturalization denial is conducted "in accordance with chapter 7 of title 5," which is a codified portion of the APA [S5].

questions.question: Do I have to go to the USCIS hearing before I can take my denial to court?
questions.answer: The provided sources indicate that exhaustion of administrative remedies is a mandatory requirement before seeking judicial review of a naturalization denial [S5]. Specifically, one source states that Section 1421(c) "requires the exhaustion of administrative remedies prior to seeking that relief" and that courts are not free to dispense with this mandatory requirement [S5]. Another source confirms that once applicants have exhausted these administrative remedies, they may appeal to a district court [S2]. Furthermore, the law provides that Section 1421(c) is the "[s]ole procedure" for applicants to challenge a denial, and such challenges must be raised in the manner prescribed by the Immigration and Nationality Act [S6].

questions.question: Does something I did before I applied count against my good moral character?
questions.answer: Yes, conduct occurring before the five-year statutory period can be considered when determining good moral character [S2]. While the statutory period for assessment is generally the five years immediately preceding the application, the Attorney General is not limited to that timeframe and may consider an applicant's conduct at any time prior to that period to determine their present moral conduct [S2]. For example, prior convictions outside the statutory period are considered relevant to determine whether an applicant has reformed [S5]. Additionally, a conviction for an aggravated felony at "any time" acts as an absolute bar to a finding of good moral character [S4]. Ultimately, good moral character is viewed as a concept derived from the "sum total of all his actions in the community" [S3].
